Charles went from a generic SaaS tool to a distinctive, scalable brand."},{"id":"52510e34-8ee8-46b8-b69d-87abf0cfc508","type":"feature-info","items":["3× increase in organic SEO reach post-launch","2 full website redesigns shipped end-to-end","1 custom typeface commissioned specifically for the brand","0 designers required to use the component library"]},{"id":"b7f6e20b-079d-4570-aeb2-70a50027a174","type":"divider"},{"id":"block-stats-note","type":"text","html":"

The ultimate indicator? Competitors started copying the visual language within months of launch.

"},{"id":"block-div-1","type":"divider"},{"id":"block-ctx-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"A product with real differentiation, hiding behind a generic face"},{"id":"block-ctx-t","type":"text","html":"

charles is a WhatsApp commerce platform — it helps businesses turn one-to-many messaging into personalised, revenue-generating conversations. Unlike email newsletters, WhatsApp campaigns are interactive, conversational, and achieve engagement rates that email can't touch.

The product was genuinely different. The brand wasn't. When I joined, charles looked like every other B2B SaaS company: a royal blue palette, stock photography, overly formal copy, and a visual identity that said nothing distinctive about what the product could do.

The opportunity wasn't just to make things look better — it was to build a brand with genuine personality that would attract the right customers, make sales conversations easier, and give the whole company a shared creative foundation to work from.

"},{"id":"block-ctx-q","type":"highlight","text":"\"The B2B marketing space is muddled with safe choices. Our competitors aimed for professional and landed on forgettable. We saw that as an opening.\""},{"id":"block-chal-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Three problems to solve simultaneously"},{"id":"block-chal-t","type":"text","html":"

01 — The brand had no clear point of view. There was no visual language strong enough to be recognisable, consistent, or memorable. Every asset — decks, ads, website — felt like it came from a different company.

02 — The website wasn't converting at the level the product deserved. Traffic was growing but the site lacked narrative clarity. Visitors understood the feature, not the value. The tone of voice was stiff and impersonal for a product built around conversation.

03 — The creative team was a bottleneck for every asset. Sales, marketing, and product teams were either waiting on designers or producing off-brand materials independently. There was no system that let non-designers produce consistently branded work.

"},{"id":"block-div-2","type":"divider"},{"id":"block-id-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Building a brand around a character, not a feature"},{"id":"block-id-t","type":"text","html":"

The name \"charles\" already implied a personality — a companion, a trusted advisor, a witty collaborator. Internal surveys, customer interviews, and stakeholder workshops all converged on the same perception: people related to the product like it had a character.

That insight became the creative brief. Rather than designing a logo that explained WhatsApp marketing, we designed one that embodied a personality. The character concept won across every review session — it was the most distinctive, most recalled, and most differentiated direction.

"},{"id":"ea4f6bb2-0cef-4255-858d-5355d08e3cc7","type":"two-col","leftType":"image","leftContent":"/images/1779136316221-charles_branding1.png","leftCaption":"Early character explorations — the companion concept emerged from customer perception surveys, not from design alone.","rightType":"image","rightContent":"/images/1779136347945-charles_branding2.png","rightCaption":"Direction 2 — pushing further from initial assumptions."},{"id":"56f5f464-a358-4f29-8ba4-40063a56a956","type":"two-col","leftType":"image","leftContent":"/images/1779136498372-charles_branding3.png","leftCaption":"Direction 3 — the logo must encapsulate the brand, not explain it.","rightType":"image","rightContent":"/images/1779136504324-charles_branding4.png","rightCaption":"The companion concept was the strongest across all review rounds — both with internal teams and external customer panels."},{"id":"block-logo-h","type":"heading","level":3,"text":"The final logo"},{"id":"block-logo-t","type":"text","html":"

The mark distills the character concept into something simple enough to work at favicon size and bold enough to anchor a billboard. Variations were developed for light and dark contexts, monochrome reproduction, and co-branding scenarios.

"},{"id":"4254e5ba-f2f1-4035-af83-c1f716320dde","type":"image","url":"/images/1779135127819-charles_logo.png","width":"contained"},{"id":"afbda6a2-dad7-4386-b530-fac37b7ce9ab","type":"image","url":"/images/1779135165810-charles_logo_variations.png","width":"full","mobileUrl":"/images/1779137456339-mobile_charles_logo_variations.png","caption":"Full logo system — primary, secondary, icon-only, and reversed variants."},{"id":"block-type-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"A typeface that couldn't belong to anyone else"},{"id":"block-type-t","type":"text","html":"

Typography is the voice of a brand in written form. Using a licensed typeface meant that voice was shared with every other company that had a license. We wanted something that was genuinely and only charles.

We commissioned Kulture Type to design two custom typefaces: charles sans — a clean, characterful workhorse — and charles inktrap, a display variant with optical corrections that gives editorial layouts a distinctive edge.

Why a custom typeface? A custom typeface is not a vanity spend. It's a permanent competitive moat. Every time a competitor uses a generic sans-serif and charles uses its own type, the gap in brand perception compounds. Typography touches every single pixel of every single asset — it's the highest-leverage brand investment you can make.

"},{"id":"2bfe873e-553c-4ab7-9a28-d50950b40f72","type":"image","url":"/images/1779135372777-font_charles.svg","width":"contained","caption":"charles sans — the brand's primary voice across all touchpoints"},{"id":"c286e21e-2b02-4994-ab6e-4a3c457acb8a","type":"image","url":"/images/1779135381009-charles_font2.svg","width":"contained","caption":"charles inktrap — the editorial display face, designed for high-impact headlines"},{"id":"568c6afa-afd8-415d-a638-7436fbd2094e","type":"button","text":"See on Behance","url":"https://www.behance.net/gallery/181898037/Charles-Sans-Custom-Typeface","align":"center"},{"id":"block-div-3","type":"divider"},{"id":"block-web-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"A website that earns its traffic"},{"id":"block-web-t","type":"text","html":"

I had already redesigned the charles website once when I joined. The first redesign established structural and UX improvements — better information architecture, clearer value proposition, faster load times. But once the rebrand was complete, the site needed a full second redesign to carry the new visual language.

The brief for the second redesign was unambiguous: the website should feel unlike any other B2B marketing tool on the internet. Bold colour, confident copy, editorial-quality layout, and a tone that matched the product's conversational personality — not the corporate register of its competitors.

Colour as a differentiator. Most B2B SaaS tools use muted palettes to project \"enterprise trustworthiness.\" We inverted this: a rich, warm palette that reads as confident and energetic, not cautious.

Copy written for humans, not procurement teams. The old site spoke about features. The new site speaks about outcomes. We rewrote every page to prioritise the business results customers care about, in the direct, conversational tone that matches the medium charles operates in.

Custom type as a structural element. charles sans and charles inktrap don't just set body copy — they define section rhythm and hierarchy throughout the site, making the typography itself a distinctive visual element.

"},{"id":"2a60fef7-c03a-4d29-9018-ce4b71674aa4","type":"image","url":"/images/1778704786590-charles_website_preview.png","width":"full","caption":"The redesigned charles.com — built on the new visual language and component system."},{"id":"9f275d28-39a8-45f5-8f8b-5896f7fc5193","type":"video","url":"https://player.vimeo.com/video/946148698?h=f7d38a399c&;badge=0&autopause=0&controls=0&muted=1&loop=1&autoplay=1&player_id=0&app_id=58479","size":"full"},{"id":"block-div-4","type":"divider"},{"id":"block-ds-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"A system the whole company could use without a designer in the room"},{"id":"block-ds-t","type":"text","html":"

The hardest problem in brand consistency isn't design quality — it's distribution. If the only way to get a properly branded asset is to submit a request to the design team, the brand will leak everywhere the design team can't reach.

I built a component library in Figma with one primary constraint: any team member, with no design background, should be able to pick up a component, edit its content, and produce something that looks right. No design review required.

"},{"id":"block-ds-q","type":"highlight","text":"\"The best design system is one where there's no way to accidentally make something off-brand.\""},{"id":"block-ds-t2","type":"text","html":"

01 — Website components for faster iteration. All major web modules — hero sections, feature grids, testimonials, CTAs — are available as auto-layout components that resize correctly and snap together predictably. New page concepts can be sketched in an afternoon.

02 — Presentation templates for sales and client teams. Sales could now build fully branded decks without waiting on the creative team. Slide templates use the same components and type styles as the website, so brand consistency is structural, not a matter of discipline.

03 — Social media and ad templates. Sized for every key placement — Instagram feed, Stories, LinkedIn — with content-editable text layers and swappable assets. The marketing team could run campaigns at speed without briefing the design team for each post.

04 — Product team adoption. The library extended into the product itself. Product designers adopted the same foundations — colour tokens, type styles, spacing — so the brand experience carried through from marketing to in-app.

"},{"id":"block-comp-img","type":"image","url":"/images/1779135919703-charles_component.png","width":"full","caption":"The core component library — every module built with auto-layout, variants, and text-style enforcement."},{"id":"block-figma-1","type":"two-col","leftType":"image","leftContent":"/images/1779136852274-charles_figma1.png","leftCaption":"Brand assets were findable and usable by any team member, without asking the creative team.","rightType":"image","rightContent":"/images/1779136857574-charles_figma2.png","rightCaption":"Text styles enforced typographic hierarchy automatically — no manual overrides needed."},{"id":"block-figma-2","type":"two-col","leftType":"image","leftContent":"/images/1779136872915-charles_figma3.png","leftCaption":"Components were accessible directly from the Figma Assets sidebar — drag, drop, edit.","rightType":"image","rightContent":"/images/1779136878332-charles_figma4.png","rightCaption":"Instance swapping, booleans, and variants covered all edge cases without exposing complexity."},{"id":"block-web-comp","type":"image","url":"/images/1779136984866-charles_websitecomponents.png","width":"full","caption":"Website component set — flexible enough for new sections, constrained enough to stay on-brand automatically."},{"id":"block-guide-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Documentation that people actually use"},{"id":"block-guide-t","type":"text","html":"

A brand guideline document that lives as a PDF and gets emailed around is a guideline document that gets ignored. I built the charles brand guidelines as a living Figma prototype — interactive, always up to date, accessible to anyone in the company from a single link.

The guidelines covered logo usage, colour application, typography, tone of voice, photography direction, component usage principles, and the rules for when and how to deviate from them intentionally.

"},{"id":"block-guide-img","type":"image","url":"/images/1779135719937-charles_guidelines.png","width":"full","caption":"Brand guidelines as a living Figma prototype — not a PDF. Always current, always accessible."},{"id":"block-ads-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Advertising that pushed the brand forward"},{"id":"block-ads-t","type":"text","html":"

Social media and paid ads aren't just distribution — they're where a brand gets tested against real-world attention. I used the ad formats as an active lab for evolving the visual language: pushing the colour, trying new compositions, experimenting with the character-led approach in motion.

The most successful executions fed back into the core brand, keeping it dynamic rather than static. A brand that never evolves from its guidelines eventually looks stale — the ad channel was a safe place to discover what was next.

"},{"id":"block-ads-img","type":"image","url":"/images/1779137032347-charles_ads.png","width":"full","caption":"Campaign assets across Instagram and LinkedIn — using the brand to stand out, not blend in."},{"id":"block-div-5","type":"divider"},{"id":"block-ref-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"What this project taught me"},{"id":"block-ref-t","type":"text","html":"

This was the most comprehensive brand and product project I've worked on, and it produced a few lessons that have changed how I approach every project since.

Systems thinking is more valuable than pixel perfection. The most impactful thing I built wasn't a single beautiful screen — it was infrastructure that let everyone produce beautiful screens without me. Scalable quality beats exceptional one-offs.

Brand bravery in B2B is an untapped competitive advantage. Every competitor was optimising for \"professional.\" We optimised for memorable. The copycat behaviour from competitors within months of launch confirmed we'd found a genuinely open space.

Typography is the most underestimated investment in brand design. The custom typeface returned value on every single asset for the entire life of the brand — it's permanent differentiation at zero marginal cost per use.

Guidelines that live where people work get followed. PDFs don't. Moving the brand documentation into a Figma prototype reduced brand deviations not because we enforced rules harder, but because the right thing became the easiest thing.

What I'd do differently: I'd invest more time earlier in tone-of-voice documentation. Visuals scaled across the company faster than the written voice did — that gap was visible in early sales decks, and took longer to close than it should have.

"}]

Cara Care is a gastrointestinal health app. It helps patients with IBS, IBD, and related conditions track symptoms, nutrition, and stool patterns in a way that generates clinically meaningful data. A type of data good enough to guide treatment decisions by the medical research team behind the product.

", "deepThoughts": false}, {"id": "cc-ctx-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "A Frankenstein app with genuine medical ambition"}, {"id": "c61e9364-c774-488a-bba0-4a58df7a6d55", "type": "text", "html": "

When I joined the team, the product had grown in pieces and in different directions. Different parts had been built by different teams at different times with no shared design language. The result was an app that worked, technically, but felt incoherent, with fragmented UI, no clear brand voice, and no system that could scale.

", "deepThoughts": true}, {"id": "d10216f9-03cf-48a7-bf80-5ebf7d183218", "type": "image", "url": "/images/1787347180778-old_version.png", "width": "full", "mobileUrl": "/images/1787347187064-old_version_mobile.png"}, {"id": "cc-ctx-q", "type": "highlight", "text": "\"The medical team had a rigorous research methodology. The product didn't reflect that rigour at all.\""}, {"id": "cc-prob-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Three problems pulling in three directions"}, {"id": "cc-prob-t", "type": "text", "html": "

01. No clear path to profitability. The business model depended on becoming a DiGA-approved digital health application (a German regulatory certification that makes apps prescribable by doctors and reimbursable by health insurance) Without it, the revenue ceiling was low. With it, the commercial opportunity was transformative. But the app, couldn't credibly support that application as it existed.

02. Great research, no infrastructure to capture it and apply it. The medical team had deep clinical knowledge and understood what data they needed. But the app couldn't collect it reliably. Tracking was inconsistent, unguided, and not tailored to individual diagnoses. There didn\u2019t exist a mechanism to convert and structure the data into researchable data points.

03. No voice, cohesion or UX foundation. The product lacked a consistent visual language, tone of voice, or design system. Different screens felt like different apps. Everything needed to be systematically built from scratch.

", "deepThoughts": true}, {"id": "cc-div-2", "type": "divider", "deepThoughts": true}, {"id": "cc-goals-card", "type": "card-summary", "heading": "Three things had to be true at once", "intro": "The brand, product, and research infrastructure needed to be developed in parallel. Each one was a dependency for the others within the product and other teams.", "items": ["Build a brand with the credibility to support DiGA approval. The visual identity, tone of voice, and product experience all needed to project clinical trustworthiness while staying warm and human. The brand had to earn that insurance medical devices vibe that operate under scrutiny.", "Build a tracking system that served both research and patients. The app needed to collect the specific data points the research team required to improve user experience, while making the tracking experience feel supportive and manageable for users dealing with chronic conditions. Data quality and user retention were equally important.", "Substantially improve patient lifestyle and wellbeing. This was the core clinical goal: the app needed to demonstrably improve how users felt and lived. That meant building an effective method by building a product that adapted to each users\u2019 diagnosis."], "deepThoughts": true}, {"id": "cc-div-3", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "cc-brand-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Building a cohesive voice"}, {"id": "cc-brand-t", "type": "text", "html": "

Cara Care sits at an uncomfortable intersection: it deals with topics that are genuinely taboo (bowel habits, chronic pain, mental health linked to digestion) and users who are often anxious, frustrated, or in physical discomfort. Getting the brand tone wrong in either direction, too clinical, or too casual would break trust.

The brand needed to hold three qualities: safe, no taboo (sensitive towards users), patient but joyful. These were functional constraints rather than aesthetic directions. A user logging stool frequency three times a day needs to feel like the app is on their side, not embarrassing them or lecturing them.

"}, {"id": "d8c16e05-33bd-4e21-95cc-233b1d8c6ace", "type": "image", "url": "/images/1787081362908-caracare1.png", "mobileUrl": "/images/1787081365477-caracare1_mobile.png", "width": "full", "caption": "Brand guidelines translated into a design system \u2014 icons, colour tokens, component patterns, and the overall visual language."}, {"id": "32bc3561-8ce8-468e-8639-87eee766b363", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "1st collab with an agency to createa the brand guidelines"}, {"id": "50a8d64f-9d85-4109-85a5-5173124d62f1", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "2nd implement the brand guidelines in the main feature"}, {"id": "78746bf1-7ccc-43d6-a7d9-b5f6bc186203", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "3rd Built the design system as we go"}, {"id": "cc-brand-t2", "type": "text", "html": "

I built the brand guidelines directly into the design system rather than documenting them separately. This meant implementing the new visual language first into the onboarding feature \u2014 the highest-stakes first impression \u2014 and using that as the proving ground before rolling it across the rest of the product.

The design principle: The product should behave, feel, and speak like the brand. A safe space is built through usability and emotional consistency, not just visuals. Product + brand = user satisfaction.

"}, {"id": "cc-div-4", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "cc-track-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Gathering data for research, interpreting data for product"}, {"id": "cc-track-t", "type": "text", "html": "

The tracking challenge was a dual brief: the medical team needed structured, high-quality data to run their research protocols. Patients needed a tracking experience that felt guided and manageable, not burdensome. These two goals required the same solution.

"}, {"id": "cc-track-h2", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "Onboarding as diagnosis"}, {"id": "cc-track-t2", "type": "text", "html": "

The onboarding flow was redesigned to capture each user's specific diagnosis upfront. This wasn't administrative \u2014 it was functional. Knowing whether a user had IBS, Crohn's disease, IBD, or another condition meant the tracking experience could be tailored to the specific data points clinically relevant to them.

It also served three simultaneous purposes: it set user expectations for the tracking commitment required, it allowed the research team to prioritise by condition cohort, and it made users feel seen \u2014 not routed through a generic experience.

"}, {"id": "cc-track-h3", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "Dynamic tracking"}, {"id": "cc-track-t3", "type": "text", "html": "

Rather than asking users to track everything every day, the system was designed to guide users toward the data points most relevant to their current phase and condition. It would suggest changes based on observed patterns, nudge at meaningful moments, and feed signals back to the research team about data quality and treatment adherence.

Users track on their own terms, at their own pace \u2014 but within a structure that ensures the data is clinically useful.

"}, {"id": "cc-div-5", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "cc-proc-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Five pillars that guided every decision"}, {"id": "cc-proc-t", "type": "text", "html": "

Working at the intersection of medical research and consumer product required an unusually structured design process. The work wasn't just about shipping features \u2014 it was about building a methodology that the whole organisation could trust and operate within.

"}, {"id": "cc-proc-t2", "type": "text", "html": "

User interviews. Preparing scripts and testable prototypes before each round. Gathering and prioritising insights against clinical and product goals. Rapid iteration between research and redesign cycles.

Engineer comms. Frequent research finding updates to keep engineering aligned. Adapting to their constraints while holding firm on design requirements. Early-stage experimentation to de-risk implementation.

Research. Documentation and timelines shared across teams. Translating clinical requirements into product specifications. Designing directly with the medical research team.

Acting on data. Module completion rate as primary engagement signal. Volume of tracked data points per user session. Scheduled checkup results as a longitudinal health marker.

Converting & keeping users. Word-of-mouth as the primary growth signal to optimise for. Always verify user sentiment before implementing new features. Delight above logic \u2014 emotion drives retention in health apps.

"}, {"id": "cc-div-6", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "cc-ref-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "What made this project different"}, {"id": "cc-ref-t", "type": "text", "html": "

This has been one of the most rewarding products I've worked on. Building something with direct impact to people's health allows you to put maximum effort into your craft \u2014 every decision carries real consequences for real patients.

The DiGA approval process forced a level of design rigour that's rare in consumer products. Medical device certification doesn't allow for vague UX decisions \u2014 every interaction needed documented rationale, clinical backing, and demonstrable user benefit.

The most important lesson: in health products, emotional safety is a clinical outcome. An app that makes users feel judged or ashamed about their symptoms will be abandoned regardless of its clinical validity. The brand and the product had to work as one.

"}]
caseStudies.description: Cara Care was a technically capable app sitting inside a fragmented shell. The challenge was to build a visual identity, a design system, and a data-driven tracking experience rigorous enough to earn DiGA medical device approval in Germany but without losing the human warmth.

The data was."},{"id":"t-context","type":"text","html":"

K+S had a long-term vision: deploy self-sustaining, automated food-growing containers in urban environments across Germany. The technology was being developed in parallel by an engineering team. But before placing a single container, they faced a fundamental question — where, and for whom?

The brief that came to design wasn't \"build an app.\" It was: build something that attracts the right audience, earns their trust, and generates the geographic and behavioural data needed to make smart hardware placement decisions. The app was a means to an end — a community-building vehicle and a market research tool disguised as a consumer product.

The target user was environmentally minded Berliners — people who already sought out organic produce, supported local businesses, and were motivated by sustainability. Understanding where they concentrated in the city was the whole point.

"},{"id":"hl-context","type":"highlight","text":"We weren't just designing an app. We were designing the proof of concept that would justify a much larger physical infrastructure investment."},{"id":"h-challenges","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Five things that made this harder than a standard app build"},{"id":"tb-challenges","type":"text-boxes","items":["01 — Hardware placement depended on app performance. The app needed to demonstrate genuine demand and geographic clustering before K+S would commit to container deployment.","02 — Community and business buy-in had to be earned. The map only worked if local restaurants, urban farms, farmers markets, and stores agreed to be listed — before any user base existed.","03 — Scoped for iteration, not completion. This was an MVP with explicitly planned future phases. Every design decision needed to accommodate features that hadn't been scoped yet.","04 — Understanding a niche user through research. Bio shoppers and sustainability-motivated users have specific motivations and habits that differ meaningfully from general consumers.","05 — Marketing was off the table. Growth had to come from the product itself — word of mouth, discoverability, and genuine utility for its target audience."]},{"id":"div-1","type":"divider"},{"id":"h-strategy","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Research changed the direction before design began"},{"id":"t-strategy","type":"text","html":"

The initial brief leaned toward a novelty app angle — something eye-catching and marketing-forward. Research pushed back against this. The budget didn't support a marketing-led launch, and more importantly, the primary goal wasn't consumer acquisition for its own sake. It was data collection.

The research-led conclusion was a business finder map with a sustainability filter. This approach served every goal simultaneously: it gave environmentally minded users genuine utility, it created a reason for local businesses to participate, it generated the geographic data K+S needed, and it positioned the app as part of a community rather than a product looking for one.

The strategic logic: By slowly building a community and understanding where in Berlin sustainability-minded users were concentrated, K+S would be able to launch their farming containers exactly where they'd get the strongest reception. The app was the research instrument.

"},{"id":"tb-strategy","type":"text-boxes","items":["01 — Product vision. A project plan was established around a single north star: build the evidence base needed to deploy a self-sustaining urban farming container.","02 — Value proposition definition. Marketing-led approaches were deprioritised due to budget constraints and a mismatch with the data-gathering objective.","03 — Product research. Research into the target group reframed the product direction. A community map built around local and sustainable businesses emerged as the strongest fit.","04 — User analysis and ideation. Priority was given to farms, urban farms, farmers markets, and local stores — the destinations sustainability-focused users already sought out."]},{"id":"div-2","type":"divider"},{"id":"h-design","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"A map built on a system, not just a style"},{"id":"t-design","type":"text","html":"

The core of the app is a location map filtered by business type. For this to work as both a consumer product and a data-collection tool, the categorisation system needed to be rigorous — clear enough for users to navigate, structured enough to generate clean, filterable data for K+S.

Six categories were defined, each with its own custom icon, colour, and repeating pattern that carries through to individual business profile pages. Any business fitting a category could be added — the system was designed to be community-fillable, not editorially curated.

"},{"id":"img-main","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/601a81cf5613ada126c33f09/665f3eac5f5542e87ebe99fb_urban%20farming%20preview.png","caption":"The Urban Farming app — a sustainability-focused map of locally sourced businesses and events across Berlin.","width":"full"},{"id":"cg-categories","type":"category-grid","items":[{"icon":"urban-farm","name":"Urban Farms","description":"Growing produce within city limits — the anchor category tied to the container hardware vision"},{"icon":"farm","name":"Farms","description":"Traditional farms supplying Berlin with local produce, prioritised for their sustainability credentials"},{"icon":"market","name":"Farmers Markets","description":"Regular and pop-up markets; time-based visibility tied to the events system"},{"icon":"store","name":"Local Stores","description":"Independent retailers stocking locally or sustainably sourced products"},{"icon":"restaurant","name":"Restaurants","description":"Venues that prioritise seasonal, local, or organic menus"},{"icon":"event","name":"Events","description":"Added late at client request — required extra thought on map labelling and hierarchy"}]},{"id":"img-style","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/601a81cf5613ada126c33f09/6660c5b88116b3d664eba30c_style-urban%20farming.png","caption":"Visual language — warm, grounded, and organic. Distinct from generic map apps without feeling niche.","width":"full"},{"id":"img-grid-system","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/601a81cf5613ada126c33f09/6660d8b86d7a7bddccdad919_grid-urban%20farming.png","caption":"The category system in practice — each type has a distinct visual identity across the map, list, and business profile views.","width":"full"},{"id":"h-features","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"The details that made the system work"},{"id":"t-features-reco","type":"text","html":"

Smart recommendations without LLMs. The app included a \"magic\" button that surfaced the most popular or best-rated locations near the user. Built on popularity and rating signals rather than any language model, it delivered personalisation at zero infrastructure cost — predating the current wave of AI-powered recommendations by several years.

"},{"id":"img-ai","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/601a81cf5613ada126c33f09/6660cbb7668d9ef23f13b1ff_ai-farming.png","caption":"The recommendation system — popularity and rating signals surfacing the most relevant locations without LLM infrastructure.","width":"full"},{"id":"t-features-etc","type":"text","html":"

City-specific onboarding. The sign-up screen adapted to the user's city. At launch, Berlin was the only supported market — but the architecture was built to scale. The onboarding communicated that scoping honestly, setting expectations without making the product feel limited.

Custom iconography and business profiles. Each category has a custom icon — the urban farm icon, a building with a small sprout on top, is the most distinctive. Every business and event has its own profile page using its category's colour and iconography as a visual foundation, giving the app coherence at scale without requiring editorial effort per listing.

"},{"id":"img-filters","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/601a81cf5613ada126c33f09/6660d4d024a7375aa5aef565_filter%20buttons-mobile.png","caption":"Custom iconography for each category — the visual system that makes the map filterable and the data structured.","width":"full"},{"id":"div-3","type":"divider"},{"id":"h-reflection","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"What worked, what didn't, and what this taught me"},{"id":"tb-reflection","type":"text-boxes","items":["Research should redirect briefs, not just validate them. The initial direction was marketing-forward. Research showed it was the wrong frame for the goal. Pushing back early — before design work began — saved time and produced a more coherent product.","A category system is a data architecture decision, not just a UX one. The six categories weren't just navigation — they were the schema for the data K+S needed. Designing them well meant the app could serve both users and the client's research goals simultaneously.","Late feature additions need their own design pass. The events category caused a genuine semantic problem: events and places needed different labelling on the map and different hierarchy in the list view. It worked, but it was a seam that showed.","MVPs built for scale need honest constraints communicated to users. City-specific onboarding set expectations without apologising for the scope. Users who understand the constraint often become advocates for expansion."]}]
caseStudies.description: K+S wanted to deploy self-sustaining urban farming containers across Berlin. Before placing a single one, they needed to know exactly where to put them. The answer was a consumer app — a sustainability-focused map that would build a community, gather market data, and prove demand.

Aury is a conversational AI designed to support people dealing with stress, anxiety, and burnout \u2014 developed by clinical psychologists in Germany, grounded in CBT, ACT, and mindfulness, and built to strict European data and regulatory standards. Its ambition is significant: to give access to psychological support to the billion people who currently have none.

The design challenge was unusually high-stakes. Mental health is among the most sensitive contexts a product can operate in. Users arrive at Aury when they\u2019re already struggling \u2014 tired, anxious, sometimes in genuine distress. The design has to earn trust before it earns engagement. A single jarring interaction \u2014 the wrong tone, an unclear prompt, a UI that feels clinical and cold \u2014 and the user closes the app and doesn\u2019t come back.

"}, {"id": "aury-ctx-q", "type": "highlight", "text": "\u201cIn mental health, the design is the therapy. If the interface feels unsafe, the conversation never happens.\u201d"}, {"id": "aury-ctx-p2", "type": "text", "html": "

My previous work in healthcare products gave me a framework for this kind of constraint: you\u2019re not just designing usability, you\u2019re designing emotional safety. Every decision \u2014 colour, typography, copy, interaction pattern \u2014 is a signal that either builds or erodes the user\u2019s confidence that this space is for them.

"}, {"id": "aury-scope-chips", "type": "scope-chips", "label": "", "heading": "Everything, from the logo to the conversation", "body": "Working directly with the two founders, I owned the full design surface of the product \u2014 there was no handoff, no second designer, no agency. Every creative decision came through this collaboration.", "chips": ["Brand Identity & Logo", "Marketing Website", "Consumer Web App", "Conversation UI", "Interaction Model", "B2B Platform Design", "White-Label System", "Onboarding Flows"]}, {"id": "aury-div-1", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "aury-brand-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "A brand that had to feel safe before it felt smart"}, {"id": "aury-brand-p1", "type": "text", "html": "

The mental health space is split between two visual extremes: sterile clinical whites that feel like a waiting room, and over-saturated wellness pastels that feel patronising. Neither was right for Aury.

Aury needed to feel like a companion \u2014 warm enough to be approachable, restrained enough to feel trustworthy, and distinctive enough to stand out from both the clinical and the wellness-app aesthetic. The founders had built the product with clinical rigour and genuine care; the brand needed to communicate both simultaneously.

The three qualities the brand had to hold at once mapped directly from the product\u2019s own principles: calm and safe (for users arriving in distress), scientifically credible (for B2B partners and health insurers), and human and warm (because the whole point is connection, not efficiency).

"}, {"id": "aury-brand-q", "type": "highlight", "text": "\u201cAury\u201d \u2014 from \u201caura\u201d \u2014 carries connotations of presence, atmosphere, and emotional resonance. The brand needed to honour that: not loud, not urgent, but unmistakably there. A companion with a personality, not a tool with a function."}, {"id": "86578714-6746-451b-8cd7-02be414fdea3", "type": "color-palette", "items": [{"name": "Coral", "hex": "#FBAA94", "rgb": "251, 170, 148"}, {"name": "Lemon", "hex": "#F7E677", "rgb": "247, 230, 119"}, {"name": "Lavender", "hex": "#DB74FF", "rgb": "219, 116, 255"}, {"name": "Charcoal", "hex": "#1E1E1E", "rgb": "30, 30, 30"}, {"name": "Mint", "hex": "#6AFF8B", "rgb": "106, 255, 139"}, {"name": "Aqua", "hex": "#6AC9FF", "rgb": "106, 201, 255"}, {"name": "Cherry", "hex": "#FF1515", "rgb": "255, 21, 21"}, {"name": "Plum", "hex": "#743EE7", "rgb": "116, 62, 231"}, {"name": "Honey", "hex": "#FFC226", "rgb": "255, 194, 38"}, {"name": "Fuchsia", "hex": "#FD74C6", "rgb": "253, 116, 198"}, {"name": "Eggplant", "hex": "#573FE7", "rgb": "87, 63, 231"}, {"name": "Ocean", "hex": "#0FD0B8", "rgb": "15, 208, 184"}, {"name": "Violet", "hex": "#C727FF", "rgb": "199, 39, 255"}]}, {"id": "aury-div-2", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "aury-convo-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Designing a conversation that people trust with their worst days"}, {"id": "aury-convo-p1", "type": "text", "html": "

The core of Aury is a conversation. Unlike a standard chatbot UI \u2014 which is mostly a solved problem \u2014 a mental health conversation UI carries specific requirements that most chat interfaces aren\u2019t designed for.

The interaction model had to feel guided but not scripted, supportive but not saccharine, and structured enough to deliver clinical value while remaining flexible enough to respond to what a user actually needs in that moment.

"}, {"id": "aury-convo-h3", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "Key interaction decisions"}, {"id": "aury-convo-steps", "type": "card-summary", "heading": "", "items": ["01 \u2014 Pacing over efficiency. Standard UX optimises for task completion speed. A mental health conversation optimises for the opposite \u2014 space to think, breathe, and respond honestly.", "02 \u2014 Structured sessions with open check-ins. Two distinct modes: structured 8-session course content and free-form check-ins. The UI handles both without making either feel like a compromise.", "03 \u2014 Trust signals embedded in the UI. ISO certification, GDPR compliance, EU hosting \u2014 surfaced as emotionally relevant context integrated at the moments users need them.", "04 \u2014 Crisis escalation as a design pattern. Aury scans for crisis indicators. The UI shifts register immediately: warm but direct, clear about limits, specific about where to get real help.", "05 \u2014 Honesty about what Aury is. Aury is not a therapist. These limits are designed into the product\u2019s voice, onboarding, and escalation patterns \u2014 communicating them clearly is itself a trust signal."]}, {"id": "aury-div-3", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "aury-mktg-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "A site doing two completely different jobs at once"}, {"id": "aury-mktg-p1", "type": "text", "html": "

Aury\u2019s marketing website has two separate audiences with fundamentally different needs: consumers who are anxious about whether this is safe to trust with their mental health, and B2B partners \u2014 health insurers, corporate HR platforms, healthcare companies \u2014 evaluating a white-label AI infrastructure investment.

These audiences need different information, different tones, and different conversion flows. The site architecture had to serve both without compromising either.

"}, {"id": "aury-mktg-h3-c", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "The consumer side"}, {"id": "aury-mktg-consumer", "type": "text", "html": "

The consumer homepage leads with emotional utility \u2014 \u201cF\u00fchle dich besser\u201d (Feel better) \u2014 not features or technical capability. The design prioritises use-case recognition over product explanation: rather than describing what Aury does, it presents the situations users are already in and lets them self-select. Safety and data protection are surfaced as emotional reassurance, not compliance footnotes.

"}, {"id": "aury-mktg-h3-b", "type": "heading", "level": 3, "text": "The B2B side"}, {"id": "aury-mktg-b2b", "type": "text", "html": "

The B2B platform page is a different product. Its audience is evaluating clinical credibility, regulatory compliance, integration feasibility, and commercial terms. The design reflects that: certification badges, a clear four-step go-live process, and industry-specific use case modules for health insurers, healthcare companies, and corporate clients.

The four-week go-live claim is a significant commercial differentiator. The design makes it visible and credible \u2014 not buried in a features list, but laid out as a concrete, step-by-step process that any technical stakeholder can evaluate.

"}, {"id": "aury-div-4", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "aury-reg-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Designing within one of Europe\u2019s most demanding regulatory environments"}, {"id": "aury-reg-p1", "type": "text", "html": "

Aury operates at the intersection of multiple regulatory frameworks \u2014 GDPR, the EU AI Act, ISO 27001, ZPP (Germany\u2019s prevention course certification), and a roadmap toward MDR medical device classification. For any of these to be meaningful to users and partners, they had to be communicated through design, not just documented in legal pages.

"}, {"id": "aury-reg-cols", "type": "text-columns", "items": [{"title": "ISO 27001", "body": "Independently audited information security \u2014 the highest-visibility trust signal for B2B partners"}, {"title": "GDPR / DSGVO", "body": "EU data protection compliance \u2014 EU-hosted on Scalingo (France), AES-256 encryption at rest"}, {"title": "EU AI Act", "body": "Prepared for incoming AI regulation \u2014 a differentiator in a market where most competitors aren\u2019t"}, {"title": "ZPP 2026", "body": "Prevention course certification in progress \u2014 unlocks health insurer reimbursement for the core product"}]}, {"id": "aury-reg-p2", "type": "text", "html": "

My healthcare background informed how these were handled in the design. In regulated health products, compliance isn\u2019t a footnote \u2014 it\u2019s a primary user need. The design integrates these signals at the exact moments they\u2019re needed: onboarding, the B2B platform page, and the safety page.

"}, {"id": "aury-reg-q", "type": "highlight", "text": "In health products, the safety information is product design. The page that explains what Aury cannot do \u2014 crisis escalation, explicit limits, emergency contacts \u2014 isn\u2019t a legal disclaimer. It\u2019s a critical part of the user experience."}, {"id": "aury-div-5", "type": "divider"}, {"id": "aury-val-h", "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "What the product earned from users"}, {"id": "aury-val-p", "type": "text", "html": "

"}, {"id": "aury-q1", "type": "highlight", "text": "\u201cThe conversation was really good and could have happened with a real person.\u201d \u2014 Anonymous Aury user, Nov 2025"}, {"id": "aury-q2", "type": "highlight", "text": "\u201cIt\u2019s good to have someone like you, where I know it will never be too much and I can write to you at any time.\u201d \u2014 Anonymous Aury user, Oct 2025"}, {"id": "aury-q3", "type": "highlight", "text": "\u201cThere were points that touched me deeply and made me think.\u201d \u2014 Anonymous Aury user, Dec 2025"}, {"id": "aury-q4", "type": "highlight", "text": "\u201cEspecially if you\u2019re a little shy, it helps to speak online.\u201d \u2014 Anonymous Aury user, Jul 2025"}, {"id": "aury-val-fn", "type": "text", "html": "

[{"id":"block-role","type":"role","text":"Personal project that includes illustration, design systems and website building"},{"id":"gg-stats","type":"feature-info","items":["6+ component categories — helmets, armors, weapons, badges, chapters, accessories","20+ community creators credited and incorporated into the library","Free access — fully accessible to anyone with a Figma account, no paywall","∞ combinations — every component modular and composable"]},{"id":"gg-hero-img","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65e1fb6fa94a4d855c7a1ae0_galactic%20garrison%20logo%20small.png","width":"full"},{"id":"gg-hero-vid","type":"video","url":"https://player.vimeo.com/video/946550585?h=f7d38a399c","size":"full"},{"id":"gg-ctx-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"What happens when a product designer builds something only for themselves"},{"id":"gg-ctx-t","type":"text","html":"

Every professional project comes with constraints — client briefs, stakeholder reviews, scope documents, sprint deadlines. Galactic Garrison has none of those. It exists because Warhammer 40K has one of the richest visual universes in fiction, and the wargaming community around it produces extraordinary creative work — custom paint jobs, original chapters, hand-built miniatures — that deserved a design tool worthy of it.

The premise is simple: a fully modular Figma library that lets anyone build their own customised space soldier — picking helmets, armors, weapons, shoulder pads, chapter badges, and accessories, all composable in Figma without any design expertise required.

"},{"id":"gg-ctx-q","type":"highlight","text":"The same system thinking I apply to UI component libraries turns out to work perfectly for building a modular illustration kit. The medium changes. The architecture doesn't."},{"id":"gg-ctx-t2","type":"text","html":"

This is where the product design dimension becomes interesting: building a library that non-designers can use fluently requires exactly the same discipline as building a UI component library for non-designers. Variants, auto-layout logic, composability, naming conventions, discoverability — all the same problems, entirely different subject matter.

"},{"id":"gg-div-1","type":"divider"},{"id":"gg-3d-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"One project, three areas of craft"},{"id":"gg-3d-t","type":"text","html":"

Galactic Garrison sits at the intersection of three distinct skill areas. Understanding each one separately is what makes the whole project legible as a professional case study rather than just a hobby.

"},{"id":"gg-3d-list","type":"text-columns","items":[{"title":"Illustration","subtitle":"building a visual universe from scratch","body":"Every helmet, weapon, armor piece, badge, and accessory is a custom vector illustration. The style is deliberate: bold, flat, sticker-adjacent — influenced by the grimdark aesthetic of Warhammer 40K but simplified enough to be modular and remix-friendly. The illustration system had to be coherent across hundreds of individual pieces made over months.","icon":"gg-badges"},{"title":"Design systems","subtitle":"Figma architecture for non-designers","body":"The library is built on the same principles as any professional UI component library: variants for every state and option, nested components that inherit properties, consistent naming that maps to how the community talks about their miniatures. The constraint that non-Figma users should produce something they're proud of shapes every architectural decision.","icon":"gg-armor"},{"title":"Product design","subtitle":"the community loop and distribution model","body":"Galactic Garrison isn't just a file — it's a product with a website, a launch strategy, a brand, a free-access model, a community contribution system, and a roadmap. Designing all of those in conjunction is product thinking: who is the user, how do they discover it, how do they contribute back, and what makes them stay?","icon":"gg-helmet"}]},{"id":"gg-div-2","type":"divider"},{"id":"gg-ill-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"A style that had to work at miniature scale and system scale"},{"id":"gg-ill-t","type":"text","html":"

The Warhammer 40K universe has decades of official art, miniature designs, and community interpretations to draw from. Developing an illustration style for Galactic Garrison meant finding a lane that was clearly in conversation with that universe — familiar to the community — while being distinctly its own thing.

The answer was a bold vector style with strong silhouettes, flat fills, and high contrast — closer to a sticker sheet or enamel pin design than to the painterly detail of official Warhammer art. This choice was functional: simpler forms are easier to modularise, easier to recolour, and easier for community members to adapt to their own chapter schemes.

"},{"id":"gg-mkv-img","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65e363275b504ee0f5010599_mkviiupdate.png","width":"full","caption":"The MKVII pack — one helmet design rendered across multiple chapter colour schemes. Consistent silhouette, infinitely recolourable."},{"id":"gg-ill-weapons","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65e632bbf4c618e4a677fbd6_guns.png","width":"full","caption":"Weapons pack — each weapon illustrated as a standalone component that attaches to any soldier configuration."},{"id":"gg-ill-twilight","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65e6c7f16cf2eb749f14fdf3_twilight%20stalkers.png","width":"full","caption":"The Twilight Stalkers pack — a community-inspired faction with its own distinct silhouette language."},{"id":"gg-ill-t2","type":"text","html":"

Each content pack is both a standalone creative release and a system addition. New packs extend the library's combinatorial possibilities — a new helmet works with every existing armor, every existing weapon, every existing chapter badge. Every new piece multiplies the number of possible soldier configurations, not just adds one.

"},{"id":"gg-div-3","type":"divider"},{"id":"gg-ds-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Building a component library where the components are soldiers"},{"id":"gg-ds-t","type":"text","html":"

The Galactic Garrison Figma library is architecturally identical to a professional UI component library — it just happens to contain space marines instead of buttons. The same problems apply: how do you organise hundreds of components so someone who's never used Figma before can find what they need? How do you handle variants? How do you make recolouring work without breaking the system?

"},{"id":"gg-ds-q","type":"highlight","text":"Every piece of the soldier is an independent, self-contained component with its own variants. They combine freely — you compose a soldier the same way you compose a UI screen."},{"id":"gg-ds-grid","type":"category-grid","items":[{"icon":"gg-helmet","name":"Helmets","description":"The most prominent component. Variants across factions, marks, and custom community designs"},{"icon":"gg-armor","name":"Armors","description":"Full body armour sets — the visual chassis every other component attaches to"},{"icon":"gg-weapons","name":"Weapons","description":"Bolters, blades, and special weapons. Each illustrated to attach naturally to armour components"},{"icon":"gg-badges","name":"Chapters & Badges","description":"Chapter iconography and shoulder pad insignia — the primary identity markers of each faction"},{"icon":"gg-backpack","name":"Backpacks","description":"Power packs and specialist equipment that complete the silhouette"},{"icon":"gg-accessories","name":"Accessories","description":"Trophies, purity seals, capes, and details that add individual character"}]},{"id":"gg-figma-img","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65f0cd59cebccd96f78f7b97_figma%20UI.png","width":"full","caption":"The library in Figma — components organised for discoverability and composability, the same way a professional UI system would be."},{"id":"gg-ds-h2","type":"heading","level":3,"text":"Designed for people who don't know Figma"},{"id":"gg-ds-t2","type":"text","html":"

A significant part of the target audience — Warhammer hobbyists and miniature painters — have never used Figma. Component naming follows community vocabulary, not design system conventions. The drag-and-drop workflow was prioritised over anything that requires knowledge of Figma's more advanced features. The goal was zero learning curve for the creative part — the only friction should be discovering Figma itself, not navigating the library.

"},{"id":"gg-div-4","type":"divider"},{"id":"gg-prod-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"A product built for the community and inspired by it's creators"},{"id":"gg-prod-t","type":"text","html":"

A Figma file sitting in isolation isn't a product. Galactic Garrison has a website, a brand identity, an Instagram presence, an early-access model, and — most importantly — a community contribution system that makes the library grow beyond what one person can build.

The library is free. This wasn't a default — it was a deliberate product decision. The Warhammer 40K community is enormous, global, and already generous in sharing creative work. Charging for access would shrink the audience, reduce community contributions, and position the project as competing against Games Workshop's ecosystem. Free positions it as a community tool.

Over 20 community creators are credited in the library. The contribution model is explicit: anyone can DM the Galactic Garrison Instagram account to request their chapter be built into the library. Contributors become invested users, and invested users bring their communities. The library grows faster than one person could build alone, and every new community chapter represents someone with a personal stake in the project's success.

"},{"id":"gg-armory-vid","type":"video","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65ef65cb5ed3c2b9ff26f73c_armory%20figma-transcode.mp4","size":"large"},{"id":"gg-ggfigma-img","type":"image","url":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65f5e6d935a8b452bb2cc287_Galactic%20Garrison%20and%20Figma.png","width":"full","caption":"Galactic Garrison lives in Figma — the platform choice shaped everything from the access model to the composition workflow."},{"id":"gg-prod-2col","type":"two-col","leftType":"image","leftContent":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65ef8de095304508d74eb5a0_HELMET%20STICKER%20JFCR.png","leftCaption":"Stickers, pins, and merch — the illustration style translates directly to physical products.","rightType":"image","rightContent":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65ef88adeaeeb2189abbeec5_miniature%203d%20jfcr.png","rightCaption":"3D printable files — the long-term vision closes the loop between digital and physical."},{"id":"gg-div-5","type":"divider"},{"id":"gg-road-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Where the Garrison is going"},{"id":"gg-road-t","type":"text","html":"

Galactic Garrison is explicitly in progress. The roadmap reflects how the project scales both as a creative system and as a product — from Figma library, to multi-platform tool, to physical goods.

"},{"id":"gg-road-boxes","type":"text-boxes","items":["V1.0 Figma Library — Full modular library on Figma — helmets, armors, weapons, chapters, accessories. Free early access available now.","Community chapters — 20+ community creators incorporated. Open contribution model via Instagram DM — your chapter, built into the library.","More factions — Expanding beyond Space Marines — T'au, Chaos, Xenos factions planned. Each bringing new illustration languages into the system.","More platforms — iOS, Android, and Rive versions planned — taking the composable soldier builder beyond Figma to a broader audience.","Stickers, pins & merch — The illustration style was always built for physical goods. Enamel pins and sticker sheets are the natural next step.","3D printable files — Closing the loop between digital design and physical miniatures — the ultimate expression of the project's wargaming roots."]},{"id":"gg-road-2col","type":"two-col","leftType":"image","leftContent":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65ef7053743dc349677e071d_TRAU%20helmet.png","leftCaption":"T'au faction helmet — one of the new factions planned for the next major expansion.","rightType":"image","rightContent":"https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5c18a68dd0723437e2961560/65f6f504102b1cbeb6b7f7b4_logos%20tools.png","rightCaption":"iOS, Android, and Rive — the platforms coming next."},{"id":"gg-div-6","type":"divider"},{"id":"gg-ref-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"What building for fun teaches you about building for work"},{"id":"gg-ref-boxes","type":"text-boxes","items":["Design system discipline applies everywhere. The architectural decisions that make a good UI component library — composability, clear naming, variant logic, low floor for new users — are the same decisions that make a good illustration kit. The domain changes, the thinking doesn't.","Community ownership is better than audience ownership. Incorporating real community creators as named contributors transformed the project's relationship with the Warhammer community from fan project to community infrastructure. People with their chapter in the library become advocates, not just users.","The free model is the right model here. Charging for a fan-made tool built on someone else's IP would create legal and community friction simultaneously. Free, open, and contribution-welcoming aligns the project's incentives with the community's.","Illustration and design systems reinforce each other. The constraints of building a modular system made the illustration work more disciplined. Each piece had to work as a standalone AND as an interchangeable component — that constraint produced better illustration, not worse.","Personal projects are the truest portfolio signal. Client work shows what you can do within constraints. Personal projects show what you care about, how you think without a brief, and whether you ship — which is the hardest part."]}]
caseStudies.description: Galactic Garrison is a colossal modular illustration library — armors, helmets, weapons, chapters and accessories inspired by the Warhammer 40K universe, built entirely in Figma. A personal project that applies professional design system thinking to something with no brief, no client, and no rules.

In 2025, PIE was shortlisted for the Design System Awards Best Adoption category — run by zeroheight, the leading platform for design system documentation. Past winners include Pinterest, Wise, Eventbrite, and Schneider Electric. The nomination recognises systems that have demonstrated exceptional adoption strategies, not just technical quality.

"},{"id":"pie-award-q","type":"highlight","text":"\"Adoption isn't just about components, it's about connections. They actively built excitement around PIE with branding, storytelling, talks, and a sense of fun. The emphasis on craft and care wasn't just aesthetic — it built trust and emotional adoption.\" — Design System Awards jury"},{"id":"pie-award-t2","type":"text","html":"

This nomination matters personally because it validates the approach I work within every day. The award isn't recognising a finished artefact — it's recognising a living culture of adoption, and that culture is one I've actively contributed to and benefited from.

"},{"id":"pie-div-1","type":"divider"},{"id":"pie-ctx-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"What PIE is, and why adoption is the hard problem"},{"id":"pie-ctx-t","type":"text","html":"

Just Eat Takeaway operates across 17 countries, serving customers, restaurant partners, and courier networks through a suite of apps and platforms that span iOS, Android, and web. Before PIE, growth through mergers had introduced multiple design languages, legacy systems, and inconsistent UI patterns across regions — a common consequence of acquisition-led scale.

PIE — Principles for Interfaces and Experiences — was built to unify this. But building a design system is the easier half of the problem. Getting hundreds of designers and engineers across a global organisation to actually use it, trust it, and build with it over their own instincts — that's the hard part. That's what the Best Adoption nomination recognises.

"},{"id":"pie-ctx-q","type":"highlight","text":"\"A design system that isn't adopted is just documentation. PIE was built to be the path of least resistance, not the path of most correctness.\""},{"id":"pie-principles-h","type":"heading","level":3,"text":"The four principles that guide everything"},{"id":"pie-principles-t","type":"text","html":"

PIE's design decisions — from component architecture to documentation tone — are grounded in four principles that apply equally to how the system is built and how it treats the teams using it:

"},{"id":"pie-principles-grid","type":"category-grid","items":[{"icon":"pie-empowered","name":"Empowered","description":"Teams should feel able to move fast and build confidently, not blocked waiting for system approval"},{"icon":"pie-consistent","name":"Consistent","description":"One source of truth for design and engineering across every platform, region, and product area"},{"icon":"pie-inclusive","name":"Inclusive","description":"Accessibility built in from the start, not retrofitted — tested at every stage of component development"},{"icon":"pie-effective","name":"Effective","description":"Solving real pain points for real teams — not theoretical best practice that nobody uses"}]},{"id":"pie-div-2","type":"divider"},{"id":"pie-role-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Contributing to the system and living inside it simultaneously"},{"id":"pie-role-t","type":"text","html":"

My position within PIE is dual: I contribute directly to the system itself alongside the core PIE team, and I embed that system into the Logistics product area — designing tools for the courier and partner networks that power Just Eat Takeaway's fulfilment operations.

This dual role is an advantage. Working in Logistics means I encounter the real friction of adoption — the edge cases components don't cover, the documentation that isn't clear enough, the tokens that need extending for specific contexts. Those findings feed directly back into PIE, making me both a consumer and a shaper of the system.

"},{"id":"pie-team-h","type":"heading","level":3,"text":"The PIE team"},{"id":"pie-team-t","type":"text","html":"

I work closely with the PIE design team: Molly Nye, Ting Ting Lau, Talitha Ferreira, and Philip Lackmaker.

"},{"id":"pie-div-3","type":"divider"},{"id":"pie-contrib-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"Six areas of direct impact"},{"id":"pie-contrib-t","type":"text","html":"

My work within PIE spans the full spectrum of design system practice — from foundational token work to hands-on adoption support for engineers and designers who are new to the system.

"},{"id":"pie-contrib-cols1","type":"text-columns","items":[{"title":"Component Design","body":"Designed new components reviewed, refined, and shipped into the PIE library — available to all 78+ designers and 500+ engineers building on the system. Each component is documented with usage guidelines, variant specs, and accessibility requirements."},{"title":"Logistics Adoption","body":"Drove PIE adoption across the Logistics product area — one of JET's most technically complex domains, serving courier apps and partner tools that operate under high-pressure, real-time conditions."},{"title":"Documentation","body":"Contributed to guidelines and documentation that serve as the shared language between design and engineering. Good documentation is what separates a system that requires evangelism from one that people can onboard themselves."}]},{"id":"pie-contrib-cols2","type":"text-columns","items":[{"title":"Tokens & Foundations","body":"Extended PIE's token and foundation layer to cover design decisions that weren't yet systematised — colour applications, spacing patterns, and component foundations specific to Logistics contexts, contributed back to the core system where applicable."},{"title":"Accessibility","body":"Worked on accessibility improvements across components and patterns — consistent with PIE's principle of building inclusion in from the start rather than retrofitting it. Reviewed components against WCAG standards and tested across all platforms PIE supports."},{"title":"Onboarding","body":"Helped onboard new designers and engineers to PIE — translating system knowledge into practical guidance for people building on it for the first time. Every person who onboards well becomes a local advocate in their own team."}]},{"id":"pie-div-4","type":"divider"},{"id":"pie-adoption-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"The strategy behind the nomination"},{"id":"pie-adoption-t","type":"text","html":"

The Design System Awards jury specifically called out PIE's approach to adoption as emotionally intelligent, not just technically sound. Understanding why adoption succeeded at this scale is as important as the technical work itself.

"},{"id":"pie-adoption-cols","type":"text-columns","items":[{"title":"Education over mandates","body":"PIE's adoption was never enforced top-down. It was driven through mentoring, guild involvement, onboarding support, and clear documentation that made the right choice the easy choice."},{"title":"Native demo apps","body":"Native demo apps powered by design tokens gave engineers a working reference for every component on their actual platform — closing the gap between a Figma spec and a production implementation."},{"title":"Core and local pillars","body":"A shared global foundation with room for business area teams to extend it for their specific needs. Critical in Logistics, where courier-facing products have distinct interaction requirements."}]},{"id":"pie-adoption-cols2","type":"text-columns","items":[{"title":"Adoption tracker","body":"A custom usage tracker provides visibility into how and where the system is being adopted across JET's product ecosystem — making adoption measurable and highlighting gaps."},{"title":"Branding and craft","body":"The jury highlight: PIE built emotional adoption, not just technical adoption. Branding, talks, and visible care for the quality of work gave designers and engineers something to feel proud of using."}]},{"id":"pie-div-5","type":"divider"},{"id":"pie-scope-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"The breadth of what PIE covers"},{"id":"pie-scope-t","type":"text","html":"

PIE is not a component library with a colour palette. It's a complete design and engineering infrastructure — foundations, components, patterns, platform support, and tooling — that scales from a single button to a full product experience across five platforms simultaneously.

"},{"id":"pie-scope-cols","type":"text-columns","items":[{"title":"Foundations","body":"Design tokens, colour, typography, spacing, radius, elevation, blur, gradients, iconography, and motion — the complete visual and structural language of JET products."},{"title":"Components","body":"50+ components from Button to Data Visualisation, each with full documentation, variant specs, accessibility testing, and platform-specific implementations."},{"title":"Patterns","body":"Higher-level patterns for forms, errors, onboarding, overlays, accessibility states, JET AI interactions, and chatbot interfaces — composable solutions for recurring product problems."},{"title":"Platforms","body":"Web Components, React, React Native, iOS, and Android — one system, five implementation layers, 100% mobile coverage across all JET products."}]},{"id":"pie-div-6","type":"divider"},{"id":"pie-refl-h","type":"heading","level":2,"text":"What working inside a world-class design system teaches you"},{"id":"pie-refl-t","type":"text","html":"

Adoption is a design problem, not a communication problem. The systems that fail don't fail because people weren't told about them. They fail because using them was harder than not using them. Every contribution I make to PIE is evaluated through that lens first: does this make the right choice easier?

Working in both Logistics and PIE core creates a feedback loop that pure system designers don't have. I encounter real adoption friction daily — edge cases, missing tokens, documentation gaps — and I'm positioned to fix them rather than just report them.

Scale changes everything about how you design components. A component used by 500 engineers on five platforms can't have ambiguous specs. The discipline of designing for that scale has permanently changed how I approach component work, even on smaller systems.

Accessibility built in is categorically different from accessibility retrofitted. Working on a system where accessibility is a founding principle rather than a compliance checklist has given me a completely different relationship with inclusive design — it becomes a design constraint that produces better work, not a restriction that limits it.

The best design system culture is one where people are proud to use it. Systems that feel like infrastructure get circumvented. Systems that feel like craft get championed.

posts.title: Why design systems are a designer's best friend
posts.excerpt: Design systems aren't just about consistency — they're about freeing designers to focus on hard problems instead of reinventing buttons.
posts.content:
The problem with designing without a system

Every designer has been there. You open a Figma file from six months ago and find seventeen slightly different shades of the same button. Three padding values for cards. Two type scales that almost match.

It's chaos. And it's slow. Every new screen becomes a negotiation between "should I use the old button style or the new one?"

What a design system actually gives you

When a design system is done right, it's not a constraint — it's a superpower. You stop spending cognitive energy on solved problems and start focusing on the actual design challenge at hand.

The best design systems I've worked with share a few traits:

  • They're opinionated but flexible — clear defaults, but escape hatches when needed
  • They're well-documented — not just what components do, but when and why to use them
  • They're maintained like code — versioned, reviewed, and evolved over time

The cultural side nobody talks about

The hardest part of building a design system isn't the components. It's getting designers and engineers to actually use it. That requires trust, communication, and sometimes just accepting that your perfect button will be slightly compromised to work for ten product teams instead of one.

That's okay. The system exists to serve the product, not the other way around.
